data.name: Port of Call
data.detailed_description:
Imagine waking up on a small dock with no recollection of who you are or how you got there. The first person you find is a grumpy, old man who enlists you to work on his ferry boat which seems to have materialized behind you. But not all is as it seems on this strange ship, and the people you meet may know more about your past than they let on.

Port of Call is a narrative exploration game that focuses on telling the player an immersive story. The game is an experiment in short-form storytelling in an immersive media. Interact with the ship's passengers and explore your surroundings in first person to try to uncover the secret of your past.

reviews.review:
Port of Call is a very short first person adventure that starts with a simple mystery. I wake up on a small dock with no idea who I am or how I got there, and the first person I meet is an old man who asks me to work on his ferry. The whole situation feels strange from the beginning because the ferry itself seems to have appeared out of nowhere. I spend the rest of the game exploring the boat, talking to the passengers and slowly trying to work out what is really going on. I like that it gives me questions early on and then lets the story gradually answer them.

The exploration is extremely simple. I walk around the ferry, look at things and talk to the different people I meet. There are no complicated puzzles or combat sections, so most of my attention goes towards the conversations and the atmosphere. I think that works because the ship itself becomes the main setting. It is small enough that I can learn where everything is, but there are still enough strange details around it to make me curious about what happened to me and why everyone seems to know more than they are saying.

The story is easily the strongest part for me. Port of Call is clearly more interested in telling a short story than giving me a huge amount of gameplay, and I think that is the right decision. The conversations slowly reveal pieces of the mystery, and some of the people on the ferry have their own reasons for being there. I like the feeling that there is something underneath the obvious situation, and the game does a decent job of keeping me interested without needing a complicated plot with loads of characters.

The biggest problem is the length. I can get through Port of Call very quickly, and once I have seen the main story there is not a huge amount left for me to do. There are seven achievements that give me a few reasons to look around more carefully, but there is no deep progression or major gameplay loop to keep me playing. I think the short length suits the story, but it also means I have to judge it more like a small interactive story than a full adventure game. If I was expecting several hours of gameplay, I would definitely be disappointed.

The presentation has also aged a bit. The environments and character models are fairly basic, and some of the movement can feel stiff compared with newer first person adventure games. I do not think that hurts the atmosphere too much because the game is more focused on the mystery than showing off its graphics. The music and sound also help create a quiet and slightly unsettling feeling, especially when I am walking around the ferry without really knowing what is happening. I think playing with headphones makes the whole thing more enjoyable.

What I appreciate most is that Port of Call does not try to stretch its idea into something bigger than it needs to be. It is a short narrative experience, and I can finish it without having to deal with filler missions, complicated systems or pointless collectibles. The ferry setting gives it a nice identity, and the mystery is enough to keep me interested until the end. I just wish there was a little more interaction and maybe some extra scenes or endings to give me more reason to return after finishing it once.

Overall, Port of Call is a small and atmospheric adventure that I think works better when I treat it as a short story rather than a conventional game. I like the mysterious opening, the ferry setting, the strange passengers and the gradual reveal of what is really happening. The extremely short length, simple interaction and dated presentation keep it from reaching the higher part of my rating scale, but I still think it is worth playing for what it is. It is free, it has a clear identity and it gives me a short mystery that does not waste my time.

Rating: 7/10
